items.stem: Which of the following best describes "audience"?
options: A question asked for effect rather than to obtain an answer, often to provoke thought or imply a point
The people a text is intended for, whose knowledge, values and expectations shape the writer's choices
The circumstances in which a text is read or viewed, which may differ from those in which it was produced
The writer's choice of words, including their connotations, formality and specificity
items.answer: The people a text is intended for, whose knowledge, values and expectations shape the writer's choices
items.markingKey: B. "audience" is the people a text is intended for, whose knowledge, values and expectations shape the writer's choices.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student delegate at an international youth climate summit.

Delegates, I was born in 2008. In my lifetime the sea outside my grandmother's house in Tuvalu has crept forty metres closer. Forty metres. You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps. You tell us we are the future. But we are not the future – we are the present, standing in water. So do not applaud me. Applause is cheap. Act.

What is the writer trying to achieve in this speech? Support your answer with evidence.
items.answer: To challenge leaders to move from symbolic gestures, such as applause for young speakers, to concrete climate action. Supporting feature: "Act." (imperative) – the final one-word command shifts responsibility to the audience with blunt force.
items.markingKey: To challenge leaders to move from symbolic gestures, such as applause for young speakers, to concrete climate action. Supporting feature: "Act." (imperative) – the final one-word command shifts responsibility to the audience with blunt force. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a language-learning app, published in an in-flight magazine.

[Image: a grandmother and a teenage boy laugh across a kitchen table in Lisbon; steam rises from two cups.]
She never learned English. He never learned Portuguese. Until now.
Fifteen minutes a day. That's all it takes to turn 'Olá' into a conversation.
Lingo Bridge – because some words can't wait for a translator.
Download free. First month on us.

Explain how the writer signals who the intended audience is.
items.answer: Travellers and members of multilingual or diaspora families (in-flight magazine readers), especially adults separated from relatives by language.
items.markingKey: Travellers and members of multilingual or diaspora families (in-flight magazine readers), especially adults separated from relatives by language. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following post by a fitness influencer on a photo-sharing platform.

5 a.m. Rain. Didn't want to. Did it anyway. [flexed-biceps emoji]
Here's the thing nobody tells you: motivation is a myth. Discipline is a decision.
Link in bio for my 30-day reset plan (only 40 spots left!!)
#grindseason #nooffdays #mindset – 214k likes

Explain one way in which the context in which this text appears affects its message.
items.answer: Influencer culture blends personal posts with marketing; high like counts act as social proof.
items.markingKey: Influencer culture blends personal posts with marketing; high like counts act as social proof. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: "A text has only one purpose." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Many texts have primary and secondary purposes – an advert may inform and entertain while its main purpose is to persuade.
items.markingKey: Many texts have primary and secondary purposes – an advert may inform and entertain while its main purpose is to persuade. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following photograph and caption from a contemporary documentary series on fast fashion, described in words.

[A young woman sits at a sewing machine in a long row of identical machines under flickering fluorescent light. In the blurred foreground lies a heap of bright T-shirts with price tags reading '4.99'.]
Caption: 'Shift 2 of 2. Rina, 19, sews 120 collars an hour.'

How might knowledge of the context of production help a reader to interpret this documentary photograph?
items.answer: Fast fashion relies on low-wage garment production; documentary photography has been used to campaign for workers' rights.
items.markingKey: Fast fashion relies on low-wage garment production; documentary photography has been used to campaign for workers' rights. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Knowing the context of a non-literary text is more important than close reading of its language."
items.answer: Both are needed, but on Paper 1 context is usually inferred from close reading, so language analysis is the route to context.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: context explains purpose and audience; misreading context leads to misinterpretation. Arguments against: Paper 1 texts are unseen and context must be inferred from the language; close reading reveals how meaning is made. Supported judgement: Both are needed, but on Paper 1 context is usually inferred from close reading, so language analysis is the route to context.

items.stem: Compare how two non-literary texts you have studied address different audiences on the same issue.
items.answer: Indicative content: identifies each audience and evidence; compares register, tone and appeals; evaluates effectiveness for each audience.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: identifies each audience and evidence; compares register, tone and appeals; evaluates effectiveness for each audience.

items.stem: Which term matches this description: "The level of formality of language, chosen to suit audience, purpose and context"?
items.answer: register
items.markingKey: B. This is the definition of register.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a student delegate at an international youth climate summit.

Delegates, I was born in 2008. In my lifetime the sea outside my grandmother's house in Tuvalu has crept forty metres closer. Forty metres. You measure progress in decades; we measure it in doorsteps. You tell us we are the future. But we are not the future – we are the present, standing in water. So do not applaud me. Applause is cheap. Act.

Identify the device used in "we are the present, standing in water" and explain its effect.
items.answer: Metaphor: "we are the present, standing in water" – it overturns the cliché "you are the future" and makes the crisis immediate and physical.
items.markingKey: Metaphor: "we are the present, standing in water" – it overturns the cliché "you are the future" and makes the crisis immediate and physical. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Explain the difference between mood and tone.
items.answer: Tone is the writer's attitude conveyed by language; mood is the feeling the text creates in the reader. A sardonic tone may create an amused or uneasy mood.
items.markingKey: Tone is the writer's attitude conveyed by language; mood is the feeling the text creates in the reader. A sardonic tone may create an amused or uneasy mood. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Amara writes: "Using lots of technical device names makes an analysis stronger." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Precise terminology helps (criterion D) but marks depend on analysing effects; a list of names without effects stays in the lower markbands.
items.markingKey: Precise terminology helps (criterion D) but marks depend on analysing effects; a list of names without effects stays in the lower markbands. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: "Rhetorical devices are only found in speeches." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Rhetorical devices appear in adverts, columns, letters and social media posts – any text that aims to persuade.
items.markingKey: Rhetorical devices appear in adverts, columns, letters and social media posts – any text that aims to persuade. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following homepage of a fictional university in Singapore, described in words.

[Banner photograph: four smiling students of different ethnicities walk across a sunlit lawn; one carries a robotic arm.]
Headline: 'Shape What's Next.'
Menu bar: Study | Research | Life on Campus | Apply Now – 'Apply Now' is an orange button, the only coloured item.
Scrolling ticker: 'Ranked #1 in Asia for graduate employability*'.
Pop-up chat window: 'Hi! I'm Ava, your student guide. What would you like to discover today?'

Analyse how the phrase "Ranked #1 in Asia for graduate employability*" contributes to the writer's purpose.
items.answer: Superlative claim: "Ranked #1 in Asia for graduate employability*" – a ranking appeals to parents' concern with careers; the asterisk hints at qualifications.
items.markingKey: Superlative claim: "Ranked #1 in Asia for graduate employability*" – a ranking appeals to parents' concern with careers; the asterisk hints at qualifications. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Tone is the single most important feature to analyse in a persuasive text."
items.answer: Tone is a useful organising idea, but strong analysis explains how specific choices create it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: tone shapes the reader's relationship with the writer; a misjudged tone can undermine persuasion. Arguments against: tone is produced by diction, syntax and structure, which must be analysed; visual and structural features may matter more in multimodal texts. Supported judgement: Tone is a useful organising idea, but strong analysis explains how specific choices create it.

items.stem: Write a 250-word persuasive paragraph for a school newsletter arguing for a later start to the school day, using at least three rhetorical devices. Then annotate each device and its intended effect.
items.answer: Indicative content: clear argument for the audience (parents/students); devices such as rhetorical question, tricolon, statistic, anecdote; annotation explains effects. Assessed for persuasiveness, control of register and accuracy of annotation.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: clear argument for the audience (parents/students); devices such as rhetorical question, tricolon, statistic, anecdote; annotation explains effects. Assessed for persuasiveness, control of register and accuracy of annotation.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "call to action".
items.answer: A closing instruction that tells the reader what to do, common in adverts and campaigns
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a closing instruction that tells the reader what to do, common in adverts and campaigns. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Explain why the placement of information at the end of a text can be powerful.
items.answer: End position gives emphasis – the reader leaves with that idea – so writers place punchlines, calls to action or key words last.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: End position gives emphasis – the reader leaves with that idea – so writers place punchlines, calls to action or key words last. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following photograph and caption from a contemporary documentary series on fast fashion, described in words.

[A young woman sits at a sewing machine in a long row of identical machines under flickering fluorescent light. In the blurred foreground lies a heap of bright T-shirts with price tags reading '4.99'.]
Caption: 'Shift 2 of 2. Rina, 19, sews 120 collars an hour.'

Explain how the caption naming the worker contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The caption naming the worker: "Rina, 19" gives her a name and age, resisting anonymity.
items.markingKey: The caption naming the worker: "Rina, 19" gives her a name and age, resisting anonymity. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: Elena writes: "A headline simply summarises the article." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Headlines also frame and evaluate events, using connotation and word order to shape interpretation.
items.markingKey: Headlines also frame and evaluate events, using connotation and word order to shape interpretation. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Tariq writes: "Structure only matters in long texts like novels." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Even a short advert has a deliberate structure – headline, image, body copy, call to action – that guides the reader.
items.markingKey: Even a short advert has a deliberate structure – headline, image, body copy, call to action – that guides the reader. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "In non-literary texts, structure is more important than language."
items.answer: Neither dominates; analysis is strongest when it shows how structural placement intensifies language choices.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: structure controls what the reader sees first and last; layout is crucial in visual texts. Arguments against: language creates tone and connotation; structure and language work together. Supported judgement: Neither dominates; analysis is strongest when it shows how structural placement intensifies language choices.

items.stem: Why do news reports use the inverted pyramid?
options: To create suspense like a short story
So readers get the key facts first and editors can cut from the bottom
To hide the main point until the end
items.answer: So readers get the key facts first and editors can cut from the bottom
items.markingKey: C. The inverted pyramid prioritises essential information.

items.stem: Which statement reflects a reader-response approach?
items.answer: Meaning is created in the interaction between reader and text
items.markingKey: Meaning is created in the interaction between reader and text. Reader response stresses the reader's role.

items.stem: Kenji writes: "If readers can interpret texts differently, then any interpretation is valid." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Interpretations must be supported by textual evidence; openness does not mean that unsupported readings are acceptable.
items.markingKey: Interpretations must be supported by textual evidence; openness does not mean that unsupported readings are acceptable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a preferred reading and a resistant reading.
items.answer: A preferred reading accepts the meaning the text encourages; a resistant reading challenges it from a different set of values or experiences.
items.markingKey: A preferred reading accepts the meaning the text encourages; a resistant reading challenges it from a different set of values or experiences. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column on art and artificial intelligence.

Last week a machine won a regional art prize. The judges, to their credit, were embarrassed. The machine, to its credit, was not – it cannot be embarrassed, which is precisely the point. Art has never been about the finished picture alone; it is about a person risking something in public. An algorithm risks nothing. It cannot fail, so it cannot really succeed.

How might the meaning of this text change for readers with different values or experiences?
items.answer: An artist may welcome the defence of human creativity; a technologist may argue the column ignores the human who prompts and curates.
items.markingKey: An artist may welcome the defence of human creativity; a technologist may argue the column ignores the human who prompts and curates. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: A student claims: "If readers can interpret texts differently, then any interpretation is valid." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Interpretations must be supported by textual evidence; openness does not mean that unsupported readings are acceptable.
items.markingKey: Interpretations must be supported by textual evidence; openness does not mean that unsupported readings are acceptable. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Choose a text you have studied that has provoked controversy. Explain two contrasting readings and evaluate which is better supported by the text.
items.answer: Indicative content: two clearly defined readings with contexts; evidence for each; reasoned evaluation. Markband: nuanced interpretation, specific evidence, balanced judgement.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: two clearly defined readings with contexts; evidence for each; reasoned evaluation. Markband: nuanced interpretation, specific evidence, balanced judgement.

items.stem: Explain why IB examiners reward alternative interpretations in Paper 1.
items.answer: Criterion A rewards interpretation; considering more than one reading shows awareness that texts are open and that readers construct meaning.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Criterion A rewards interpretation; considering more than one reading shows awareness that texts are open and that readers construct meaning. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Define the term "audience".
items.answer: The people a text is intended for, whose knowledge, values and expectations shape the writer's choices
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the people a text is intended for, whose knowledge, values and expectations shape the writer's choices. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Outline the meaning of the term "diction".
items.answer: The writer's choice of words, including their connotations, formality and specificity
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: the writer's choice of words, including their connotations, formality and specificity. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between structure and layout.
items.answer: Structure is the organisation and sequence of ideas (opening, turn, ending); layout is the visual arrangement on the page or screen (columns, images, white space). Both shape reading.
items.markingKey: Structure is the organisation and sequence of ideas (opening, turn, ending); layout is the visual arrangement on the page or screen (columns, images, white space). Both shape reading. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following viral post shared on a messaging app.

SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS!!! My cousin's friend works at a hospital and says the new phone masts in our city are making people sick. The media won't report it. Why? Follow the money. Do your own research. [18.2k shares]

Explain how one feature of the text could be interpreted in more than one way.
items.answer: A frightened reader may share it; a media-literate reader recognises classic misinformation markers.
items.markingKey: A frightened reader may share it; a media-literate reader recognises classic misinformation markers. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Distinguish between the actual audience and the intended audience.
items.answer: The intended audience is who the writer had in mind; the actual audience is whoever reads it, including unintended readers such as students analysing it later.
items.markingKey: The intended audience is who the writer had in mind; the actual audience is whoever reads it, including unintended readers such as students analysing it later. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why identifying a device is not enough in Paper 1 analysis.
items.answer: Criterion B rewards analysis of effect: a device only matters because of how it shapes meaning or affects the audience in relation to purpose.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Criterion B rewards analysis of effect: a device only matters because of how it shapes meaning or affects the audience in relation to purpose. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following viral post shared on a messaging app.

SHARE BEFORE THEY DELETE THIS!!! My cousin's friend works at a hospital and says the new phone masts in our city are making people sick. The media won't report it. Why? Follow the money. Do your own research. [18.2k shares]

How does the instruction to share placed before the claim shape the reader's experience of the text?
items.answer: The instruction to share placed before the claim: the reader is asked to act before evaluating the information.
items.markingKey: The instruction to share placed before the claim: the reader is asked to act before evaluating the information. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following meme shared on a student forum, described in words.

[Image, top: a tiny kitten stares bravely at an enormous, overflowing laundry basket. Top text: 'ME IN SEPTEMBER: I'LL START MY IA EARLY THIS YEAR'.]
[Image, bottom: the same kitten, now buried under the laundry, only its ears showing. Bottom text: 'ME, 11:58 P.M. THE NIGHT BEFORE THE DEADLINE'.]

How might the meaning of this text change for readers with different values or experiences?
items.answer: Students laugh in recognition; a teacher might read it as a sign of workload pressure.
items.markingKey: Students laugh in recognition; a teacher might read it as a sign of workload pressure. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following donation page on an animal-rescue charity's website, described in words.

[Photograph: a one-eyed dog looks straight into the camera.]
'Meet Biscuit. He was found tied to a motorway barrier in January.'
Progress bar: 'This month: 8,450 euros of 10,000 raised.'
Buttons: 10 | 25 | 50 | Other. A pre-ticked box: 'Make this a monthly gift'.
Footer: '94 cents of every euro goes directly to animal care.'

State the main purpose of the text and explain how one feature helps to achieve it.
items.answer: To persuade visitors to donate, ideally monthly. Supporting feature: "tied to a motorway barrier in January" (emotive detail) – specific cruelty and winter cold provoke pity and anger.
items.markingKey: To persuade visitors to donate, ideally monthly. Supporting feature: "tied to a motorway barrier in January" (emotive detail) – specific cruelty and winter cold provoke pity and anger. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a family SUV, printed in a weekend newspaper magazine.

[Image: a father at the wheel, two children asleep in the back, mountains at dusk through the windscreen.]
HE'S GOT THIS.
Seven seats. Five-star safety. Zero doubts.
The Atlas X7. Built for the man who carries everyone.
[Small print: 7.9 L/100 km combined. Model shown with optional extras.]

Identify the device used in "HE'S GOT THIS" and explain its effect.
items.answer: Colloquialism: "HE'S GOT THIS" – the casual, reassuring idiom presents the father as calm and competent and invites male readers to identify with him.
items.markingKey: Colloquialism: "HE'S GOT THIS" – the casual, reassuring idiom presents the father as calm and competent and invites male readers to identify with him. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following infographic from an international water charity, described in words.

[Title in bold blue capitals: 'THE WALK'.] [A single dotted line runs right across the page and ends at a small well icon.]
Label beside the line: 'The distance many women and girls in rural areas walk for water each day: up to 6 km.'
Below: '20 litres. That's what she carries back – about the weight of a full suitcase.'
[Bottom panel: a tap icon.] 'A donation of 25 euros helps bring a tap within 15 minutes of her home.'

Explain how the title "THE WALK" contributes to the meaning of the text.
items.answer: The title "THE WALK": naming the burden as a single, definite journey gives it weight.
items.markingKey: The title "THE WALK": naming the burden as a single, definite journey gives it weight. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem:
Read the following opinion column in an English-language newspaper in Lisbon.

My grandmother's street in Alfama now has eleven bakeries and no neighbours. The bakeries sell pastéis de nata to people who will leave on Sunday; the neighbours who once bought bread there have left for good, priced out by short-term rentals. Tourism, we are told, is our salvation. Perhaps. But a city that sells its every doorway eventually has nothing left to show its visitors except itself, emptied.

How might the meaning of this text change for readers with different values or experiences?
items.answer: A resident may feel vindicated; a business owner who depends on tourism may see the column as nostalgic and one-sided.
items.markingKey: A resident may feel vindicated; a business owner who depends on tourism may see the column as nostalgic and one-sided. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following advertisement for a refillable water bottle, displayed on a city bus shelter.

YOUR 7:42 DOESN'T WAIT. NEITHER DOES THE PLANET.
[Image: a commuter's hand grips a matte-green bottle against a blurred, grey crowd.]
Every minute, a million plastic bottles are sold worldwide. You only need one.
FLOW. Steel-built. Leak-proof. Yours for life.
Fill it. Carry it. Keep it.
Refill free at 300 stations across the city – find yours on the FLOW app.

Evaluate how effectively the text is shaped for its audience and purpose in its context.
items.answer: Busy urban commuters: the time-stamped train ("Your 7:42"), the direct address and the bus-shelter placement target people travelling to work. To persuade commuters to buy a FLOW bottle by presenting the purchase as both convenient and environmentally responsible. It appears in a city at a time of public concern about single-use plastic; the free refill stations suggest a partnership with the city, so the brand looks civic-minded rather than simply commercial.
items.markingKey: Busy urban commuters: the time-stamped train ("Your 7:42"), the direct address and the bus-shelter placement target people travelling to work. To persuade commuters to buy a FLOW bottle by presenting the purchase as both convenient and environmentally responsible. It appears in a city at a time of public concern about single-use plastic; the free refill stations suggest a partnership with the city, so the brand looks civic-minded rather than simply commercial. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem:
Read the following letter to the editor of a regional newspaper in northern England.

Sir, – Your columnist last week described our local accent as 'charming but unprofessional'. I have been a nurse for twenty-two years. I have said 'you're alright, love' to frightened patients at three in the morning, and not one has asked for my vowels to be adjusted. Accent is not a skill deficit. It is where we come from, and where many of your readers still live.

Evaluate the effectiveness of the antithesis "Accent is not a skill deficit. It is where we come from" and of at least one other stylistic feature in achieving the writer's purpose.
items.answer: Antithesis: "Accent is not a skill deficit. It is where we come from" – the "not X but Y" structure redefines accent as identity and place.
items.markingKey: Antithesis: "Accent is not a skill deficit. It is where we come from" – the "not X but Y" structure redefines accent as identity and place. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a city mayor at the opening of a public library in a multilingual neighbourhood.

Friends, neighbours – bienvenidos, karibu, welcome. Some people say libraries are relics, that everything we need is on our phones. But a phone cannot hold a child's hand through her first chapter book. A phone does not stay open late for the night-shift nurse who wants to finish her degree. This building belongs to you: to every language spoken on these streets, and to every language not yet learned.

To what extent does the organisation of this text contribute more to its effect than its language? Refer to the closing tricolon of belonging and at least one language choice.
items.answer: The closing tricolon of belonging: ending with "every language not yet learned" looks to the future and makes the building a shared possession.
items.markingKey: The closing tricolon of belonging: ending with "every language not yet learned" looks to the future and makes the building a shared possession. Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: A speech delivered at a youth climate summit and later shared online has which kind of audience?
options: Only the people in the room
A primary (live) audience and a secondary (online) audience
items.answer: A primary (live) audience and a secondary (online) audience
items.markingKey: D. Texts often have multiple audiences with different expectations.

items.stem: "We shall fight on the beaches, we shall fight on the landing grounds" uses which device?
items.answer: Anaphora
items.markingKey: D. Repeating "we shall fight" at the start of successive clauses is anaphora (Churchill, 1940).

items.stem: Explain how short paragraphs affect the reader of an online article.
items.answer: They make the text easier to scan on a screen and give each point emphasis, though they may also fragment the argument.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: They make the text easier to scan on a screen and give each point emphasis, though they may also fragment the argument. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem:
Read the following speech by a campaigner for women's suffrage at a public meeting in Manchester, 1912 (an original pastiche written for study).

Gentlemen of the press, you call us unreasonable. Very well. Was it reasonable that my mother paid taxes on a shop she ran for thirty years, yet could not vote for the men who spent them? Was it reasonable that the law counted her as a citizen when it came to paying, and as a child when it came to choosing? We have asked politely for forty years. Politeness has been answered with silence. We shall not be silent any longer.

Explain why this text might be read differently by two different audiences.
items.answer: Supporters hear justified resolve; a 1912 sceptic might hear a threat; a modern reader sees a familiar strategy of reclaiming an insult.
items.markingKey: Supporters hear justified resolve; a 1912 sceptic might hear a threat; a modern reader sees a familiar strategy of reclaiming an insult. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem: Explain why the same advertisement might be interpreted differently by two audiences.
items.answer: Meaning depends on readers' contexts: values, cultural knowledge and experience lead them to read connotations and images differently.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Meaning depends on readers' contexts: values, cultural knowledge and experience lead them to read connotations and images differently. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain how connotation can carry bias in a news text.
items.answer: Words with the same literal meaning ("protesters" versus "mob") carry different associations, so a writer can steer opinion while appearing to report facts.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Words with the same literal meaning ("protesters" versus "mob") carry different associations, so a writer can steer opinion while appearing to report facts. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Distinguish between coherence and cohesion.
items.answer: Cohesion is the surface linking of sentences through connectives and reference; coherence is the overall logical sense of the text. A text can be cohesive but incoherent if its ideas do not connect.
items.markingKey: Cohesion is the surface linking of sentences through connectives and reference; coherence is the overall logical sense of the text. A text can be cohesive but incoherent if its ideas do not connect. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Read the following single-panel editorial cartoon, described in words.

[A giant smartphone towers over a family dinner table like a skyscraper. The parents and two children sit at its base, each gazing up at its glowing screen. Their plates are untouched. Under the table, the family dog looks up at the reader. Speech bubble from the dog: 'Remember when they used to drop food?']

How might the meaning of this text change for readers with different values or experiences?
items.answer: Parents may laugh guiltily; teenagers may notice the parents are just as absorbed.
items.markingKey: Parents may laugh guiltily; teenagers may notice the parents are just as absorbed. Credit any well-justified alternative supported by the text; the answer given is the most direct reading.

items.stem:
Read the following infographic from a national youth health service website, described in words.

[Headline: 'WHERE DOES YOUR PHONE SLEEP?'] [Two bars side by side: a short purple bar labelled 'Phone in bedroom: 7 h 1 min average sleep' and a taller bar labelled 'Phone outside bedroom: 8 h 3 min'.]
[Small moon icons fill the taller bar.] 'Each extra hour of evening screen time = about 15 minutes later to sleep.'
[Footer:] 'Charge it outside. Sleep inside.' Source: national youth sleep survey, 2025 (illustrative figures).

Who is the target audience of the text? Refer to two specific details that suggest this audience.
items.answer: Teenagers and their parents visiting a youth health website.
items.markingKey: Teenagers and their parents visiting a youth health website. Award marks for an accurate, specific point (criterion A: understanding and interpretation) supported by a reference to the text; a general assertion without evidence earns at most 1 mark.

items.stem: A student claims: "Using lots of technical device names makes an analysis stronger." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Precise terminology helps (criterion D) but marks depend on analysing effects; a list of names without effects stays in the lower markbands.
items.markingKey: Precise terminology helps (criterion D) but marks depend on analysing effects; a list of names without effects stays in the lower markbands. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem:
Read the following donation page on an animal-rescue charity's website, described in words.

[Photograph: a one-eyed dog looks straight into the camera.]
'Meet Biscuit. He was found tied to a motorway barrier in January.'
Progress bar: 'This month: 8,450 euros of 10,000 raised.'
Buttons: 10 | 25 | 50 | Other. A pre-ticked box: 'Make this a monthly gift'.
Footer: '94 cents of every euro goes directly to animal care.'

How does the progress bar near the goal shape the reader's experience of the text?
items.answer: The progress bar near the goal: showing the target almost reached encourages visitors to help complete it.
items.markingKey: The progress bar near the goal: showing the target almost reached encourages visitors to help complete it. Award marks for: an accurate identification of the feature, a precise reference to the text, and an explanation of its effect on the intended audience linked to purpose (criterion B). Identification without effect: half marks at most.

items.stem: "The writer's intention is the only correct meaning of a text." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Intentions are often unknowable and meaning also depends on readers and contexts; analysis focuses on effects supported by the text.
items.markingKey: Intentions are often unknowable and meaning also depends on readers and contexts; analysis focuses on effects supported by the text. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Knowing the context of a non-literary text is more important than close reading of its language."
items.answer: Both are needed, but on Paper 1 context is usually inferred from close reading, so language analysis is the route to context.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: context explains purpose and audience; misreading context leads to misinterpretation. Arguments against: Paper 1 texts are unseen and context must be inferred from the language; close reading reveals how meaning is made. Supported judgement: Both are needed, but on Paper 1 context is usually inferred from close reading, so language analysis is the route to context.

items.stem: "Tone is the single most important feature to analyse in a persuasive text." Discuss.
items.answer: Tone is a useful organising idea, but strong analysis explains how specific choices create it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: tone shapes the reader's relationship with the writer; a misjudged tone can undermine persuasion. Arguments against: tone is produced by diction, syntax and structure, which must be analysed; visual and structural features may matter more in multimodal texts. Supported judgement: Tone is a useful organising idea, but strong analysis explains how specific choices create it. Markbands (10 marks): Markbands (criteria A–D). A Knowledge, understanding and interpretation; B Analysis and evaluation of authorial choices; C Focus and organisation; D Language. Top band: an insightful, convincing interpretation supported by well-chosen references; perceptive analysis of how specific choices shape meaning and affect the audience; a sustained, coherent line of argument; precise, varied, register-appropriate academic language. Middle band: relevant interpretation and some analysis, but partly descriptive or unevenly supported. Low band: mostly summary or feature-spotting without effect.

items.stem: Rewrite the opening of a news report you have studied as an opinion column. Then explain how and why you changed its structure.
items.answer: Indicative content: first-person hook, anecdote or provocative claim; argument with concession; commentary explaining the shift from inverted pyramid to argumentative structure.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: first-person hook, anecdote or provocative claim; argument with concession; commentary explaining the shift from inverted pyramid to argumentative structure.
